meaning: One thing has just happened when, right after it, something unexpected follows. It can also describe constant change, or “I thought ..., but actually ...”.
connection: Verb た-form + かと思うと／かと思ったら (also 「かと思えば」)

senses.label: No sooner ... than
senses.meaning: The first action has only just happened when a second change follows almost at once. The second half is usually something surprising that the speaker observes. It is normally not used for the speaker's own actions.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + かと思うと／かと思ったら
examples: No sooner had the sky gone dark than it started pouring.
He'd only just come home when he went straight back out again.

senses.label: One moment ..., the next ...
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思えば／かと思うと」 links two opposite situations to show things keep changing. It can also mean “some ..., others ...”.
senses.connection: Verb た-form / dictionary form + かと思えば、〜も
examples: One moment my little sister is crying, and the next she's already laughing.
Lately there are hot days, and then there are days that suddenly turn cold.

senses.label: I thought ..., but actually
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思ったら」 can also mean the speaker assumed something, but it turned out otherwise. It carries surprise. Common in speech.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思ったら
examples: It was so quiet I thought they were studying, but they were asleep.
I thought he'd already gone home, but he was still at the office.

notes: In the “no sooner ... than” sense it cannot describe the speaker's own actions: ✕「私は家に帰ったかと思うと、すぐ寝た」→ ○「私は家に帰ると、すぐ寝た」／「家に帰ったとたん、寝てしまった」.
The second half cannot be a volitional, command, or request: ✕「授業が終わったかと思うと、すぐ帰りなさい」→ ○「授業が終わったら、すぐ帰りなさい」.

「〜かと思ったら」 can mean either “no sooner ... than” or “I thought ..., but actually ...”, depending on what comes before it: 「寝たかと思ったら、もう起きてきた」 (he'd only just fallen asleep and was already up); 「寝ているかと思ったら、起きていた」 (I thought he was asleep, but he was awake).
「〜かと思って」 means “thinking that ..., (I did ...)” and gives the reason for an action: 「雨が降るかと思って傘を持ってきた」. It does not mean “no sooner ... than”.

daily.title: Sudden weather change
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about the shower just now.
daily.example: It was sunny a minute ago, and then it suddenly started raining, huh.

daily.title: Talking about kids
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that your child can't sit still.
daily.example: My kid no sooner sits down than he's back on his feet.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's movements.
daily.example: She had barely raised her face when she left the room without a word.

work.title: Weather forecast
work.description: A presenter describes a sharp change in the weather.
work.example: This afternoon, temperatures suddenly dropped, and snow began falling in many areas.

work.title: Financial news
work.description: A report describes big swings in stock prices.
work.example: Stock prices rose for a while, only to fall sharply in the afternoon.

etymology: Made from the question particle 「か」, the quotation particle 「と」, and the conditional of 「思う」. Literally “just as I was thinking it was ...”. From this came “no sooner ... than” and “I thought ..., but actually”.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Both mean “just as ...”. 「たとたん」 can be used for the speaker's own actions (「立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした」); 「かと思うと」 normally describes changes the speaker sees in other people or things, and stresses surprise more.

similar.title: 〜か〜ないかのうちに
similar.explanation: Also describes two events happening almost simultaneously, stressing that “the second began before the first had quite finished”, so the timing is tighter: 「ベルが鳴るか鳴らないかのうちに」. With 「かと思うと」 the first event has already happened, and the point is how unexpected the second is.

similar.title: 〜と思いきや／〜かと思いきや
similar.explanation: Close to the “I thought ..., but actually ...” sense of 「かと思ったら」, and it also contains 「と思う」. 「思いきや」 is written, slightly literary, and used mostly in prose; 「かと思ったら」 is spoken.

similar.title: 〜かと思う・〜かと思った
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「か＋と思う」. 「かと思った」 alone simply states “I thought ...”; only when 「と／たら」 is added does 「かと思うと／かと思ったら」 become a connector meaning “no sooner ... than / I thought ..., but actually ...”.

formation: 「〜かと思うと」 = the question particle 「か」 + the quotation particle 「と」 + 「思う」 + the 「と」 of “as soon as ...”. 「か」 turns the first clause into a judgment the speaker has not yet confirmed, and 「と思う」 is “to think to oneself”, so literally it is “at the moment I just thought ‘has ... happened?’”. The speaker has barely registered the first event when the second is already under way. That gives “no sooner ... than”, along with a sense of watching from the sidelines and being caught off guard, which is also why it is normally not used for your own actions (you do not need to “suppose” what you yourself are doing). With 「思ったら」, if the supposition is overturned by what follows, it becomes “I thought ..., but actually ...”; with 「思えば」 setting two opposite situations side by side, it becomes “one moment ..., the next ...”.

meaning: A comparison: it isn't actually so, but it looks as if it were. Often paired with 「まるで」 or 「あたかも」.
connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjectives usually take 「である」) + かのようだ／かのように／かのような

senses.label: As if ...
senses.meaning: Compares something to what it is not. Compared with the figurative 「〜ようだ」, it stresses more that “it isn't really so”. Fairly literary, and often used with 「まるで」 or 「あたかも」.
senses.connection: Plain form + かのようだ／かのような + noun／かのように + verb
examples: It's only April, but it's as hot as if midsummer had already arrived.
The room was so quiet it was as if time had stopped.
Her smile was like a flower blooming.

senses.label: Acting as if ...
senses.meaning: Describes someone's attitude: they behave as if something were true when it isn't. Often critical or disapproving.
senses.connection: Plain form + かのように + 振る舞う・話す・言う, etc.
examples: He's acting as if he knows nothing.
She was laughing as if nothing had happened.
He talks as if he were the company president.

notes: It is used only for comparison where the facts are otherwise; it cannot be used for a grounded inference, or the meaning flips: 「彼は家にいるかのようだ」 means “he seems to be at home, but he isn't”. To say “he seems to be at home”, use 「彼は家にいるようだ」.
After nouns and な-adjectives, 「である」 is normally inserted: 「夢であるかのようだ」「本物であるかのような」. Use this connection in exams.

Sense 2 describes someone “acting as if ...” and is often critical: 「何も知らないかのように振る舞う」 implies “he knows perfectly well but pretends not to”, so saying this to someone's face amounts to accusing them of lying, which is very rude.
Use 「かのような」 before a noun and 「かのように」 to modify a verb or adjective: ✕「夢を見ているかのような笑った」→ ○「夢を見ているかのように笑った」.

daily.title: Complaining about the heat
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about a muggy summer day.
daily.example: It's so hot, it's like being in a sauna.

daily.title: Teasing a friend
daily.description: A friend shows up late but acts like nothing's wrong.
daily.example: He came late, yet he's got a face like nothing happened.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a landscape.
daily.example: Covered in snow, the town looked as if it were asleep.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report describes the scene after a disaster.
work.example: After the earthquake, the city looked as if it were a battlefield.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A column criticizes a company's attitude toward a problem.
work.example: The company went on explaining as if there had been no problem at all.

etymology: Made from the question particle 「か」, the nominalizer 「の」, and the auxiliary 「ようだ」 for likeness. 「か」 adds the sense “whether it's true is uncertain — in fact it isn't”, so the pattern is used only for comparisons.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「かのようだ」 is simply 「ようだ」 with 「か（の）」 added. 「ようだ」 can express comparison or inference (「誰か来たようだ」); 「かのようだ」 is comparison only, stresses that “it is actually not so”, and feels more literary.

similar.title: まるで〜ようだ
similar.explanation: Both mean “just like ...”, and they often combine as 「まるで〜かのようだ」. Plain 「まるで〜ようだ」 is an ordinary comparison; 「かのようだ」 highlights “it isn't, yet it looks as if it were” and is mostly used in written description.

similar.title: 〜んばかりに／〜んばかりの
similar.explanation: Also “as if about to ...”, but 「んばかり」 stresses “almost doing the action” (「泣かんばかりに頼む」) and is more exaggerated; 「かのようだ」 is a general comparison.

similar.title: 〜ふりをする
similar.explanation: Close to “pretending to ...” in sense 2. 「ふりをする」 states directly that someone is deliberately pretending; 「かのように振る舞う」 is a description from the outside, stressing “looks just like ...”, and often carries criticism.

formation: 「〜かのようだ」 = the question particle 「か」 + the nominalizer 「の」 + the comparison auxiliary 「ようだ」. 「ようだ」 alone already means “like ...”. Inserting 「か」 before it turns the first part into a proposition with a question mark, “is it ...?”, which amounts to the speaker admitting “in fact it is not so”. 「の」 nominalizes this questioned clause so that 「ようだ」 can attach to it. So 「かのようだ」 adds a layer of “I know it isn't” compared with 「ようだ」, and works only for comparison, not for inference. Used of a person's attitude, “acting as if it were so while knowing it is not” becomes “pretending that ...”.

meaning: Shows the viewpoint or standard behind a judgment: “speaking from ...” / “judging by ...”.
connection: Noun + からいうと／からいえば／からいって

senses.label: From the standpoint of ...
senses.meaning: Makes a judgment from a certain standpoint or viewpoint. Usually follows abstract nouns like 「立場」「経験」「観点」「点」.
senses.connection: Noun + からいうと／からいえば
examples: Speaking from my experience, this method is the most effective.
From a teacher's standpoint, I think homework is necessary.

senses.label: Judging by ...
senses.meaning: Makes an evaluation or inference based on a standard, data, or facts. The second half is usually the speaker's judgment.
senses.connection: Noun + からいって／からいえば (often with 「実力」「成績」「規模」)
examples: Judging by ability, he'll probably win.
In terms of population, Tokyo is Japan's largest city.

notes: A person noun cannot come directly before it, which is the most common mistake: ✕「先生からいうと、この作文はよくない」→ ○「先生からすると／先生から見ると、この作文はよくない」.
The second half is a judgment or evaluation the speaker makes from that standpoint or standard; it cannot be a request or command: ✕「経験から言って、手伝ってください」→ ○「経験から言って、一人では無理だと思います。手伝ってください」.
The 「から」 in 「部長には私から言っておきます」 shows “who will say it” (I will pass it on); it is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Comparing products
daily.description: Discussing with a friend which phone to buy.
daily.example: Price-wise, this one's the better deal.

daily.title: Giving advice
daily.description: A senior gives a junior advice from experience.
daily.example: From experience, the first year is the hardest.

work.title: Meeting discussion
work.description: Giving an opinion from a cost perspective.
work.example: In terms of cost, Plan A is more realistic.

work.title: Analysis report
work.description: A report makes a judgment based on data.
work.example: Judging by the sales trend, reaching next year's target looks difficult.

etymology: Made from the particle 「から」 (starting point or basis) + the conditional of 「言う」. Literally “if we speak from ...”, it marks the starting point of a judgment.

similar.title: 〜からすると・〜からすれば
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both mean “from the standpoint of ...”. 「からすると」 can follow a person noun to mean “in someone's view” (「親からすると」) and is also used to infer from clues; 「からいうと」 generally does not take people, and mostly takes abstract nouns like 「立場」「点」「経験」.

similar.title: 〜からして
similar.explanation: Sense 2, “judging from ...”, is close to this grammar point, and the second half is mostly a conjecture. But 「からして」 is more often used for “from ... alone (let alone the rest)”, a use 「からいうと」 does not have.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: Often compared with it: to say “for someone” use 「にとって」 (「私にとって大切な人」), followed by an evaluation; 「からいうと」 does not take people and means “from a certain standard or viewpoint”.

formation: 「〜から言うと」 = the 「から」 that marks a starting point or basis + 「言う」 + the conditional 「と／ば」 (or the te-form 「言って」). Literally, “if I speak starting from ...”: 「から」 sets the preceding noun as the starting point of what is said, 「言う」 means giving an opinion, and the conditional makes the statement the premise for the judgment that follows. It therefore naturally expresses “judging with a certain viewpoint or standard as the starting point”, and is usually preceded by abstract nouns that can serve as such a starting point, like 「立場」「点」「経験」「実力」. Because the subject of 「言う」 is the speaker, putting another person's noun before 「から」 would mean “starting from that person”, which makes no sense; to express someone else's standpoint, use 「からすると」 or 「にとって」 instead.

meaning: Picks out the most basic, typical detail: “just from this alone ... (never mind the rest)”. Also marks the basis of a judgment.

senses.label: Even just ...
senses.meaning: Picks out the most basic or minor detail and implies everything else is the same. Usually negative, but can be positive.
senses.connection: Noun + からして (often with 「名前」「態度」「服装」「入口」)
examples: Just look at his clothes — he's sloppy.
Even the entrance of this shop feels upscale.
I don't like that person — even the way they talk.

senses.label: Judging from ...
senses.meaning: Makes an inference based on a situation, like 「〜からすると」. The second half is usually a guess with 「〜ようだ」「〜そうだ」「〜だろう」.
senses.connection: Noun + からして (often with 「口ぶり」「様子」「状況」)
examples: Judging from the way he talks, he seems to know something.
Judging from the sky, it looks like it'll rain this afternoon.

notes: Sense 1 picks “the most basic, most superficial” point, implying that the deeper parts are the same; you cannot pick something that is itself the core: ✕「この料理は味からしておいしい」→ ○「この料理は見た目からしておいしそうだ」.
Sense 1 is mostly used for negative evaluation; saying 「〜からして…」 about someone's appearance or way of speaking clearly expresses distaste, and is very rude to say to their face or to a superior.
Sense 1 cannot be replaced with 「からすると」, while sense 2 (basis for judgment) can be swapped: 「服装からしてだらしない」 (sloppy from the clothes alone) ≠ 「服装からすると…」 (judging from the clothes ...).
「だからして」 is an old-fashioned conjunction meaning “therefore” and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Judging a restaurant
daily.description: Walking past a newly opened shop with a friend.
daily.example: This place looks delicious just from the sign.

daily.title: First impressions
daily.description: Talking with a friend about your impression of someone.
daily.example: I think that person is rude — even the way they say hello.

work.title: Reviewing a proposal
work.description: A boss is unhappy with a proposal.
work.example: This proposal doesn't grab me — even the title has no appeal.

work.title: Analyzing data
work.description: Drawing a conclusion from survey results.
work.example: Judging from the survey results, young people seem to have little interest.

etymology: Made from the particle 「から」 + 「して」, the te-form of 「する」. 「から」 marks the starting point and 「して」 links it on, giving “starting from ...”. This led to the uses for giving an example and for the basis of a judgment.

similar.title: 〜からすると・〜からすれば
similar.explanation: Sense 2, “judging from ...”, can be swapped with 「からすると」, and the second half is mostly a conjecture. But 「からすると」 lacks sense 1, “from ... alone, let alone the rest”.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Both can give one example that implies the rest. 「さえ」 picks an extreme, least likely example (「子供さえ知っている」); 「からして」 picks the most basic, first-seen part (「名前からして怪しい」).

similar.title: 〜にしてからが
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning: “even ... (the very thing that should be so)”, citing one representative point to imply the whole. 「にしてからが」 is a more formal, stiffer N1 expression, mostly used with people; 「からして」 has a wider range.

formation: 「〜からして」 = the case particle 「から」 marking a starting point + the te-form 「して」 of 「する」. In written Japanese 「して」 often follows a noun plus case particle for emphasis (as in 「〜にして」「〜をして」), and here it is generally taken to strengthen 「から」. Together: “starting from ... already ...”. The starting point is the most basic, outermost link; if even that is so, the deeper parts surely are too, which gives sense 1, “from ... alone”. Read the “starting point” as the starting point of a judgment and you get sense 2, “judging from ...”, which overlaps with 「からすると」.

meaning: Says you can't reach the usual conclusion from just one reason. The second half is usually negative or partly negative.
connection: Plain form + からといって (casually 「からって」)

senses.label: Just because ... doesn't mean
senses.meaning: Even if there is a certain reason, the expected result does not necessarily follow. Often followed by 「〜とは限らない」「〜わけではない」「〜とは言えない」.
senses.connection: Plain form + からといって、〜とは限らない／〜わけではない
examples: Having money doesn't necessarily make you happy.
Just because someone is Japanese doesn't mean they can use honorifics correctly.

senses.label: Just because ..., you shouldn't
senses.meaning: Followed by a prohibition or negative judgment: you shouldn't do something for that reason alone. Has an admonishing or critical tone. Casually, 「からって」.
senses.connection: Plain form + からといって、〜てはいけない／〜のはよくない
examples: Just because you don't like vegetables doesn't mean it's OK to never eat them.
Even if you're busy, you can't skip meals.

notes: The second half must be negative or partially negative; remove the negation and the meaning is completely reversed: ✕「お金があるからといって、幸せだ」→ ○「お金があるからといって、幸せだとは限らない」.
What is denied is “the conclusion drawn from this reason”, not the first half itself: 「日本人だからといって敬語が上手なわけではない」 denies “is good at keigo”, not “is Japanese”.
Colloquial 「〜からって」 is very casual and is not used to superiors or clients; 「忙しいからって休むな」 (「からって」 plus a prohibition) sounds harsh, and saying it to an elder is very rude.
Sentence-initial 「だからといって」 is a conjunction meaning “even so (that doesn't mean ...)”, and must follow a complete sentence.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend wants to give up after failing one exam.
daily.example: Just because you failed once doesn't mean you have to give up.

daily.title: Stereotypes
daily.description: A friend assumes all tall people are good at basketball.
daily.example: Just because you're tall doesn't mean you're good at basketball.

daily.title: Mom's reminder
daily.description: A mother warns her child during the holidays.
daily.example: Just because it's a holiday doesn't mean you can sleep till noon.

work.title: Boss's warning
work.description: Reminding an experienced employee not to get careless.
work.example: Just because you have experience doesn't mean you can skip the checks.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A newspaper column analyzes employment issues.
work.example: A high salary doesn't mean it's a good place to work.

etymology: Made from 「から」 (reason), the quotation particle 「と」, and 「言って」, the te-form of 「言う」. Literally “even if you say it's because ...”, which led to “that reason alone isn't enough”.

similar.title: 〜かといって
similar.explanation: Same origin, both contain 「と言って」, and the second half is mostly negative too. 「かといって」 is often used at the start of a sentence (「高いのは嫌だ。かといって安物も困る」) to mean “that's so, but the opposite is no good either”; 「からといって」 means “you cannot ... just because of this reason”.

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: Same origin, both built on 「と言う」, and both express concession. 「といっても」 corrects the preceding statement and lowers expectations (「料理ができるといっても、簡単なものだけだ」); 「からといって」 denies a conclusion drawn from a reason.

similar.title: 〜とはいえ
similar.explanation: Both mean “although ..., yet ...”. 「とはいえ」 is a written concession and the second half need not be negative (「春とはいえ、まだ寒い」); with 「からといって」 the second half must be negative or partially negative.

similar.title: 〜とて
similar.explanation: 「からとて」 is a written, slightly archaic version of 「からといって」 with the same meaning; 「とて」 alone can also mean “even ...” (「私とて人間だ」).

formation: 「〜からといって」 = the reason-marking 「から」 + the quotation particle 「と」 + the te-form 「言って」 of 「言う」. 「〜からと言う」 quotes the first clause as a “reason” being put forward, and the te-form works here as a concession, literally “even if you give ‘because ...’ as the reason”. The speaker first lays out a reason someone might offer, then rejects it in the second half: “that reason does not hold up”. The second half is therefore naturally negative or partially negative, often paired with 「とは限らない」「わけではない」. With a prohibition it becomes “don't use this as an excuse to ...”. In speech it is shortened to 「からって」.

meaning: Now that a certain situation exists, something naturally must follow. It can also draw a natural conclusion from that fact.
connection: Verb / い-adjective plain form, or noun / な-adjective + である + からには

senses.label: Now that ..., I must
senses.meaning: Now that you've done something or are in a certain position, you must see it through. The second half is usually an obligation, resolution, or advice: 「〜なければならない」「〜つもりだ」「〜べきだ」「〜たい」.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + からには
examples: Now that I've promised, I have to keep it.
If I'm going to play in the match, I really want to win.
Since I'm going to study abroad, I plan to study hard.

senses.label: Since ..., surely
senses.meaning: Draws a natural conclusion from a fact. The second half is usually 「〜はずだ」「〜に違いない」「〜だろう」.
senses.connection: Plain form + からには
examples: Since he's taken it on, he's sure to do a good job.
With a line this long, it must be a good restaurant.

notes: The second half must be the speaker's resolve, obligation, assertion, or conjecture, not an objective fact or past result: ✕「約束したからには、彼は来なかった」→ ○「約束したからには、彼は必ず来るはずだ」.
Nouns and な-adjectives need 「である」: ✕「学生からには」→ ○「学生であるからには」; 「学生からには」 alone would be read as “starting from students”.
「〜からには〜べきだ／〜なさい」 is strong when applied to others: saying 「プロであるからには、もっと努力すべきです」 to a client or superior is rude; it is mostly used to state your own resolve.
To simply state a cause, use 「から」: ✕「雨が降ったからには、試合は中止になった」→ ○「雨が降ったから、試合は中止になった」.

daily.title: Making up your mind
daily.description: Cheering yourself on when starting a new skill.
daily.example: Now that I've started, I'm going to see it through!

daily.title: Between friends
daily.description: A friend has signed up for a marathon.
daily.example: Now that you've signed up, you'd better train properly.

work.title: Taking on a project
work.description: Telling your boss you've accepted a job.
work.example: Now that I've taken on this job, I'll take responsibility and see it through to the end.

work.title: President's speech
work.description: The company president addresses new employees.
work.example: Now that you are a member of our company, please conduct yourselves as professionals.

etymology: Made from the reason particle 「から」, the particle 「に」, and the topic particle 「は」. 「からに」 is thought to have already meant “now that ...” in classical Japanese, and 「は」 adds emphasis.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning, both “since ..., then ...”, with the second half mostly an obligation, resolve, or inference. 「以上は」 is more formal and often used for rules, contracts, and formal occasions; 「からには」 is more colloquial and carries a tone of personal resolve.

similar.title: 〜上は
similar.explanation: Also “since ..., then ...”, but very literary and solemn, mostly for major decisions (「引き受けた上は全力を尽くす」). In everyday speech 「からには」 is normally used.

similar.title: 〜のだから・〜んだから
similar.explanation: Both take a fact the listener also accepts as a premise and draw an assertion from it. 「のだから」 is often used to blame or press the other person (「約束したんだから、守ってよ」); 「からには」 stresses resolve to “see it through now that we've come this far”.

formation: 「〜からには」 = the reason-marking 「から」 + the case particle 「に」 + the topic particle 「は」. 「からに」 is generally thought to have meant “since ...” already in the old language: 「に」 limits the first clause to an already established premise, and 「は」 raises it as a topic for emphasis, together meaning “given this (already established) reason”. Since the premise is settled and cannot be withdrawn, the second half naturally gives a resolve or obligation (“then I must / I will ...”) or an inference (“then surely ...”). Because it stresses how the speaker responds once the premise is fixed, the second half cannot be an objective description.

meaning: Attached to an adjective stem and so on; shows that someone looks a certain way or has a certain expression.
connection: い-adjective stem / な-adjective stem + げ; verb ます-stem + たげ; noun + ありげ

senses.label: Looking ...
senses.meaning: Shows a feeling or state that can be read from someone's face or manner. Mostly describes other people; common in writing and novels.
senses.connection: い-adjective stem / な-adjective stem + げな／げに／げだ (common: 「寂しげ」「楽しげ」「得意げ」「不安げ」)
examples: She was looking out the window with a lonely face.
The children are playing happily.
He proudly showed off his work.

senses.label: Seeming to want ...
senses.meaning: 「〜たげ」 means someone looks like they want to do something. 「〜ありげ」 means someone seems to have something (such as hidden meaning or confidence).
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たげ / noun + ありげ
examples: He looked like he wanted to say something.
She smiled meaningfully.
The new employee gave the presentation with a confident air.

notes: 「げ」 describes the look someone's appearance gives off, and is not used for the speaker's own feelings: ✕「私は寂しげだ」→ ○「私は寂しい」.
Unlike 「〜そうだ」, 「げ」 is mostly used for outwardly visible emotion or mental state, not for judging the nature of things: ✕「このケーキはおいしげだ」→ ○「このケーキはおいしそうだ」.
「大人げない」 means “(an adult) immature and lacking dignity, like a child” and is criticism; calling a superior or elder 「大人げない」 is very rude. 「危なげない」, by contrast, is praise: “steady, reliable”.
「よさげ」 and 「なさげ」 are young people's colloquial forms, not used in formal settings or written prose.

daily.title: Watching a friend
daily.description: You notice a friend seems to have something on their mind.
daily.example: What's wrong? You look like you want to say something.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's expression.
daily.example: The boy looked down sadly.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report describes the award winners.
work.example: The winners proudly held up their medals.

work.title: After a meeting
work.description: A colleague quietly comments on a client's reaction.
work.example: They seemed a little dissatisfied, didn't they?

etymology: Generally thought to come from the noun 「気（け）」 (air, appearance), voiced to 「げ」. Added to a stem, it means “the look of ...”.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: Both mean “looks ...”. 「そうだ」 has a wide range and can describe people, things, and weather (「雨が降りそうだ」「おいしそうだ」); 「げ」 mainly describes a person's expression and bearing, has a literary flavor, and is common in writing and novels.

similar.title: 〜がる・〜がっている
similar.explanation: Both describe other people's feelings. 「がる」 is about someone showing the feeling in behavior (「寂しがっている」); 「げ」 is the look read from appearance and expression (「寂しげな顔」), and is more subtle.

similar.title: 〜めく
similar.explanation: Both mean “having an air of ...”. 「めく」 follows a noun and means starting to show signs of something (「春めく」「皮肉めいた言い方」); 「げ」 follows an adjective stem and means feeling that shows in expression and bearing.

formation: 「〜げ」 is generally thought to come from the noun 「気（け）」 (air, look), voiced to 「げ」 after a stem. An adjective stem alone only states a quality; adding 「げ」 makes it “the look of giving off this air”: 「寂しげ」 = looking as if it carries an air of loneliness. 「げ」 is a nominal element, so the whole behaves like a な-adjective: 「〜げな」「〜げに」「〜げだ」. Because it describes “the air seen from the outside”, it is mostly used for other people's emotions and expressions, not the speaker's own; 「言いたげ」「意味ありげ」 work the same way, giving off an air of wanting to say something or of having a meaning.

meaning: Stresses a reason: it is precisely because of this reason (and no other) that the result follows.
connection: Plain form + からこそ (often paired with 「〜のだ／〜んです」 at the end)

senses.label: Precisely because ...
senses.meaning: 「こそ」 highlights the reason given by 「から」: “this is the real reason”. The sentence often ends with 「〜のだ」 or 「〜んです」.
senses.connection: Plain form + からこそ、〜のだ
examples: It's precisely because it's you that I want to ask you to do this job.
It was precisely because I practiced every day that I was able to win.

senses.label: Exactly because ...
senses.meaning: The first half would normally be seen as a negative reason, but the speaker turns it into a reason for positive action. Has an emphatic, unexpected tone.
senses.connection: Plain form + からこそ
examples: I scold you strictly precisely because I love you.
Precisely because I'm busy, I want to value my time off.
Some things you can only learn because you failed.

notes: Among cause expressions, only 「から」 can take 「こそ」 directly: ✕「好きなのでこそ」→ ○「好きだからこそ」.
「からこそ」 stresses what the speaker takes to be the “real reason”; for a plain, objective cause it sounds exaggerated: ✕「雨が降ったからこそ、道が濡れている」→ ○「雨が降ったから、道が濡れている」.
Do not confuse it with 「〜てこそ」: 「やってみてこそ分かる」 means “you only understand once you try” (condition); 「やってみたからこそ分かった」 means “it's precisely because I tried that I understood” (cause).

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: Thanking a friend who has always supported you.
daily.example: It's only because you were there for me that I could keep going this far.

daily.title: Parental lecture
daily.description: A mother explains why she is strict with her child.
daily.example: I'm saying this precisely because you matter to me.

work.title: Celebration speech
work.description: Speaking at a party after a project succeeds.
work.example: It's thanks to everyone's cooperation that this project succeeded.

work.title: Corporate philosophy
work.description: A company profile stresses its values.
work.example: Precisely because times are tough, we will remain committed to quality.

etymology: Made from the reason particle 「から」 + the emphatic particle 「こそ」. 「こそ」 puts the focus on the reason.

similar.title: 〜こそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「からこそ」 is simply the cause 「から」 plus the emphatic particle 「こそ」. 「こそ」 alone can emphasize any element (「今年こそ合格したい」); 「からこそ」 emphasizes the cause specifically.

similar.title: 〜ばこそ
similar.explanation: Same meaning, “precisely because ...”. 「ばこそ」 is written and slightly archaic (「子を思えばこそ厳しくする」); in everyday speech 「からこそ」 is normally used.

similar.title: 〜てこそ
similar.explanation: Also contains 「こそ」 and is often confused. 「てこそ」 stresses a condition, “only if ...”, mostly for general truths; 「からこそ」 stresses a cause, “precisely because ...”, mostly explaining the reason for a particular matter.

similar.title: 〜だけに
similar.explanation: Both show cause and result matching. 「だけに」 stresses “precisely because ..., all the more / naturally ...” (「期待していただけに、がっかりした」); 「からこそ」 stresses “this very reason, and no other”.

formation: 「〜からこそ」 = the cause conjunctive particle 「から」 + the focus particle 「こそ」. The job of 「こそ」 is to pick one out of several candidates and focus on it. Added after the cause 「から」, it picks this cause out from all possible reasons: “not anything else, precisely because of this”. Because it picks and excludes, it is often used to state a reason others would not think of, even turning a condition normally seen as negative into a reason for positive action (「愛しているからこそ叱る」). Sentence-final 「のだ／んです」 often accompanies it, further giving the explanatory tone of “this is the truth”.

meaning: Only under a certain condition does something truly happen or have real value.

senses.label: Only by ...
senses.meaning: Only by doing something can you get the result in the second half. The second half is usually positive, such as 「分かる」 or 「できる」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + こそ、〜 (potential form, 分かる, etc.)
examples: Only when you try it yourself do you understand how hard it is.
Only after hardship can you taste the joy of success.
Only by actually going there do you see what it's really like.

senses.label: Only with ... does it count
senses.meaning: Often 「〜あってこそ」 or 「〜てこそ〜だ」: only when a condition is met does something have meaning or deserve its name.
senses.connection: Noun + があってこそ / verb te-form + こそ〜だ
examples: Only when you're healthy can you enjoy your work.
I am who I am today only because of my family's support.
A promise means something only if you keep it.

notes: The result must be positive or “only then meaningful”, not a negative result: ✕「無理をしてこそ、病気になった」→ ○「無理をしたから、病気になった」.
「てこそ」 states the general truth of “only if ... then ...”; it is not used to explain the cause of one event that has already happened: ✕「昨日練習してこそ、今日勝てた」→ ○「昨日練習したからこそ、今日勝てた」.
「今でこそ」 means “now it is ... (though it wasn't before)”, a fixed expression and not this grammar point: 「今でこそ有名だが、昔は無名だった」.

daily.title: Study tips
daily.description: Sharing tips on learning a foreign language with a friend.
daily.example: You only get better at a foreign language by using it.

daily.title: Recommending a trip
daily.description: Encouraging a friend to go see it in person.
daily.example: You only understand what's great about Kyoto by walking around it yourself.

work.title: Morning meeting
work.description: A boss stresses teamwork.
work.example: Only with teamwork can we accomplish big things.

work.title: New hire training
work.description: Explaining the service philosophy during training.
work.example: Only when our customers are satisfied can we call it true service.

etymology: Made from the te-form 「て」 + the emphatic particle 「こそ」. 「こそ」 puts the focus on the condition in the first half: “only by doing ...”.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: Also contains 「こそ」 and is the easiest to confuse. 「てこそ」 stresses a condition, “only if you do ... then ...”; 「からこそ」 stresses a cause, “precisely because ...”, mostly explaining the reason for something that happened.

similar.title: 〜ないことには
similar.explanation: Expresses the same idea from the negative side: “if you don't ..., (you can't) ...”, with the second half mostly negative (「やってみないことには分からない」). 「てこそ」 says positively “only by doing it can ...”, with a positive result.

similar.title: 〜てからでないと
similar.explanation: Also “you can't ... without first ...”, but it stresses time order (「確認してからでないと返事できない」); 「てこそ」 stresses the value and meaning of the first clause.

similar.title: 〜あっての
similar.explanation: Close to 「〜あってこそ」, both “only with ... is there ...”. 「AあってのB」 is a noun-modifying form (「お客様あっての商売」) and more literary; 「あってこそ」 is followed by a clause.

formation: 「〜てこそ」 = the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the focus particle 「こそ」. The te-form links two events and implies “only after going through the first does the second come”. 「こそ」 puts the focus on the first clause: “it is precisely by going through this step that the second half holds”. Read in reverse, “without this step it will not do”, which gives the conditional emphasis “only if ... then ...”. 「あってこそ」 puts 「ある」 in, meaning “only with ... present”, and is often used to explain the premise of something's value. Since it stresses “a condition worth going through”, the second half is mostly a positive result or value.

meaning: Expresses strong emotion in the form of a rhetorical question: “how ... it was!” / “I can't tell you how many times ...”.
connection: どんなに／どれほど／何度, etc. ... verb / adjective noun-modifying form + ことか (also 「ことだろうか」)

senses.label: How ...!
senses.meaning: Exclaims how great the degree is. Often paired with 「どんなに」「どれほど」「どれだけ」「何と」.
senses.connection: どんなに／どれほど〜 + noun-modifying form + ことか
examples: How happy I was when I heard I'd passed!
How lonely it is to live alone!
How long I waited for your letter!

senses.label: Who knows how many times
senses.meaning: Paired with 「何度」「何回」「何時間」 and the like to stress how many times or how long.
senses.connection: 何度／何回／何時間 + verb た-form + ことか
examples: I can't tell you how many times I thought about quitting this job.
I waited hours and hours for him at the station!

notes: It looks like a question but is actually an exclamation; do not read it as asking: 「どれほど心配したことか」 means “how worried I was!”, not “how much did I worry?”.
It usually pairs with words of degree or number like 「どんなに」「どれほど」「何度」; otherwise it is easily heard as an ordinary question: 「どんなに嬉しかったことか」.
With a tone of reproach (「何度言ったことか」 = how many times have I told you), it blames the other person, and is very rude to a superior or client.
The 「か」 in 「どういうことか説明して」「何が起きたのか」 is a question particle and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Telling a friend how hard your early days abroad were.
daily.example: When I'd just started studying abroad, I can't tell you how many times I wanted to go home.

daily.title: A letter to your parents
daily.description: Thanking your mother in a letter.
daily.example: Mom, you have no idea how much your words encouraged me.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's inner monologue in a novel.
daily.example: How beautiful the sky was that day!

work.title: Retirement speech
work.description: Looking back on your career at a farewell party.
work.example: Over these thirty years, how much you have all helped me!

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」 + the question particle 「か」. It uses the question “just how ... was it?” to express exclamation — a kind of rhetorical emphasis.

similar.title: 〜ものだ (feeling, natural truth, reminiscence)
similar.explanation: Both can express deep feeling. 「ものだ」 is a sigh about things in general or the past (「時が経つのは早いものだ」); 「ことか」 stresses the depth of degree or number in the form of a rhetorical question, with stronger emotion.

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: Both express an extreme degree. 「といったらない」 follows a noun or adjective and means “indescribably ...” (「悔しいといったらない」); 「ことか」 often pairs with 「どんなに」「何度」 and exclaims by way of a rhetorical question.

similar.title: 〜なんという／なんと〜 (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Both are for strong exclamation. 「なんと〜のだろう」 mostly exclaims over the nature of what is before you (「なんと美しい景色だろう」); 「ことか」 mostly looks back on feelings or numbers of times you have experienced.

formation: 「〜ことか」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + the question particle 「か」. 「こと」 sums up the preceding degree or number as one “matter”, and 「か」 asks about it as a question: “just what degree is that?”. Together with question words like 「どんなに」「何度」 it becomes “just how ...?”. The speaker does not need an answer; the implication is that the degree is too high or the number too large to answer, so it becomes an exclamation in the form of a rhetorical question. Adding 「だろう」「でしょう」 makes it a conjectural question, softer and more lingering in tone.

meaning: Makes a guess based on a person's character or the nature of something that both speakers know: “it's ..., so (surely) ...”.
connection: Noun + の + ことだから

senses.label: Knowing him, ...
senses.meaning: Guesses how someone will act, based on shared knowledge of their personality or habits. Often followed by 「きっと」「〜だろう」「〜に違いない」.
senses.connection: Person noun + のことだから
examples: Tanaka's so conscientious, he'll be here on time.
Knowing him, he's overslept somewhere again.
Knowing that kid, I'm sure they'll be fine.

senses.label: After all, it's ...
senses.meaning: Follows a noun for a thing or time and makes a guess from its usual nature, or asks for understanding.
senses.connection: Noun (thing) + のことだから
examples: They're only children, so please go easy on them.
It's the end of the year, so the roads are probably crowded.

notes: What precedes must be a person or thing whose character both speaker and listener know well; saying 「あなたのことだから」 to someone you have just met would be odd.
Used for a negative inference (「彼のことだから、また遅れるだろう」) it carries a teasing, distrustful tone, and is very rude when used about a superior or client.
A person noun needs 「の」: ✕「田中さんことだから」→ ○「田中さんのことだから」.
The 「こと」 in 「大切なことだから」「大事なことですから」 means “matter” and the phrase means “because it's an important matter”; it is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Waiting for a friend
daily.description: A friend is late and everyone is guessing why.
daily.example: Knowing him, he's probably lost again, isn't he?

daily.title: Reassuring family
daily.description: A family member is worried about a child taking an exam.
daily.example: That kid is so dependable, there's no need to worry.

work.title: Evaluating a subordinate
work.description: A boss talks to a colleague about a capable team member.
work.example: Knowing Yamada, I'm sure he'll have it done properly by the deadline.

work.title: Predicting a reaction
work.description: Colleagues discuss the department head's decision-making style.
work.example: The department head is so cautious, I don't think he'll decide right away.

etymology: 「こと」 originally means “matter”, and 「〜のこと」 means “the matter of ...”. With 「だから」 (reason), it literally means “because it's a matter of ...”, and from there “since it's that person (or thing)”.

similar.title: 〜だけあって
similar.explanation: Both rely on the character of a person or thing. 「だけあって」 evaluates a known fact, “as one would expect of ...” (「プロだけあって上手だ」); 「ことだから」 is mostly for guessing at something not yet confirmed (「彼のことだから、きっと来る」).

similar.title: 〜ことだし
similar.explanation: Same origin, both built from 「こと＋だ」. 「ことだし」 follows the plain form and gives one reason as grounds for doing something (「雨も止んだことだし、出かけよう」), with the second half mostly volition or invitation; 「ことだから」 follows 「noun＋の」, and the second half is mostly a conjecture.

similar.title: 〜ことから
similar.explanation: Same origin, also drawing a judgment from a “matter”. 「ことから」 follows the plain form and gives the grounds for a name or an inference (「形が似ていることから、この名前がついた」), and is more literary; 「ことだから」 relies on the usual character of a person or thing.

formation: 「〜ことだから」 = noun + 「の」 + the formal noun 「こと」 + the reason-marking 「だから」. 「〜のこと」 originally means “matters concerning ...”, pointing to everything about that person or thing, including their usual behavior; 「だから」 takes this whole as the reason. Together: “since we are talking about that person/thing (both of us know)”, from which “then he is sure to ...” follows naturally. So what precedes must be a person or thing whose traits both parties know, and the second half is mostly an inference based on that knowledge, with 「きっと」「だろう」「に違いない」.

meaning: Written style. Means “without doing ...” or “... never happened”, like 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ずに」.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなく

senses.label: Without stopping
senses.meaning: An interruption that could have happened never did, and the state continues. Common: 「休むことなく」「絶えることなく」「変わることなく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなく〜続ける
examples: He worked from morning till night without a break.
The river flows on without end.
Their friendship continued unchanged for decades.

senses.label: Without ...
senses.meaning: Does the second action without doing the first. More written and formal than 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ずに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなく、〜
examples: She quit the company without consulting anyone.
I chose this path without hesitation.
They fought to the end without giving up.

notes: It is written language; in everyday conversation people say 「休まないで」 or 「休まずに」, and 「ことなく」 in speech sounds stiff.
The negation is already contained in 「なく」, so the preceding verb must be a positive dictionary form: ✕「休まないことなく働いた」→ ○「休むことなく働いた」; adding 「ない」 makes a double negative and reverses the meaning.
Do not confuse it with 「〜ことなしに」: 「ことなしに（〜ない）」 means “cannot ... without doing ...” (「努力することなしに成功はない」); 「ことなく」 only means “without doing ... / never having ...”.
「することなくて暇だ」 is a shortening of 「することがなくて」 (having nothing to do) and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: Seen while reading sports news.
daily.example: The team reached the final without losing a single game.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character leaving.
daily.example: He walked toward the station without looking back.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: A company makes a promise to its customers.
work.example: We will continue to improve our service without compromising on quality.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a construction project finished smoothly.
work.example: The construction was completed on schedule without a single accident.

etymology: Made from the formal noun 「こと」 + 「なく」, the continuative form of the adjective 「ない」. Literally “there being no doing of ...”.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, “without doing ...”. 「ずに」 is used in both writing and speech; 「ことなく」 is more formal and often means “something that could have happened never did” (「一度も休むことなく」).

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Same meaning; 「ないで」 is the most colloquial form. In speeches, articles, and news 「ことなく」 is common, and in everyday conversation 「ないで」 is used.

similar.title: 〜ことなしに
similar.explanation: Same origin, both built from 「こと＋ない」. 「ことなしに」 is mostly followed by a negative or difficulty, a condition meaning “cannot ... without doing ...”; 「ことなく」 merely describes doing the second half without ...ing.

formation: 「〜ことなく」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + the continuative form 「なく」 of the adjective 「ない」. 「こと」 first turns the preceding verb into a “matter”, 「ない」 says this matter does not exist, and the continuative 「なく」 links the clause to the second half, literally “in a situation where the matter of ... does not exist (do the second half)”. This “nominalize first, then negate” structure is more objective and formal than negating the verb directly (「〜ないで」), hence its written register. Nominalizing “interruption, change” and so on and then negating gives “not once ...”, stressing the continuation of a state: 「休むことなく」「絶えることなく」.
